content: Preterm infants often begin milk feeding through a gavage tube. As they grow and develop, they gradually transition to sucking feeds. Mothers of preterm infants may not always be present in the hospital to breastfeed, necessitating alternative feeding methods. The most common alternative is feeding with a bottle, using either expressed breast milk or formula. However, there is ongoing debate about whether the use of bottles during the establishment of breastfeeding negatively impacts breastfeeding success. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of avoiding bottle feeding during the establishment of breastfeeding on the likelihood of successful breastfeeding. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the safety of alternative feeding methods to bottles. A new search strategy was implemented for this review update, with searches conducted in September 2021 across databases such as MEDLINE, CENTRAL, and CINAHL, without restrictions on date or language. The ISRCTN trial registry and reference lists of retrieved articles were also searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs. The inclusion criteria were RCTs and quasi-RCTs that compared the avoidance of bottles with the use of bottles for preterm infants whose mothers intended to breastfeed. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. When necessary, study authors were contacted for additional information. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Outcomes assessed included the rates of full breastfeeding and any breastfeeding (full or partial) at discharge, three months, and six months post-discharge, as well as the length of hospital stay and the incidence of infant infections. Data were synthesized using risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and mean differences (MD), with 95% confidence intervals (CI). This updated review included seven trials involving 1,152 preterm infants. Three additional studies are awaiting classification. Among the included studies, five used a cup feeding strategy, one used a tube feeding strategy, and one used a novel teat designed to mimic the sucking action of breastfeeding. The novel teat study was included because of its design to closely replicate breastfeeding mechanics. The trials were of small to moderate size, and two studies had a high risk of attrition bias. One study reported poor adherence to cup feeding, suggesting dissatisfaction with this method among staff or parents, while the other four cup feeding studies did not report such issues. The findings suggest that avoiding bottles may increase the likelihood of full breastfeeding at discharge (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.19 to 1.80; 6 studies, 1,074 infants; low-certainty evidence). It also likely increases the rate of any breastfeeding (full or partial) at discharge (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.16; 6 studies, 1,138 infants; moderate-certainty evidence). Avoiding bottles probably increases the rate of full breastfeeding three months after discharge (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.78; 4 studies, 986 infants; moderate-certainty evidence) and may also increase full breastfeeding six months after discharge (RR 1.64, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.36; 3 studies, 887 infants; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, avoiding bottles may increase the rate of any breastfeeding (full or partial) three months after discharge (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.71; 5 studies, 1,063 infants; low-certainty evidence) and six months after discharge (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.41; 3 studies, 886 infants; low-certainty evidence). The positive effects on breastfeeding outcomes were observed at all time points for the tube feeding strategy and at all time points except for any breastfeeding at three months post-discharge for cup feeding. However, these effects were not observed for the novel teat. There were no significant differences in other outcomes, such as the length of hospital stay (MD 2.25 days, 95% CI −3.36 to 7.86; 4 studies, 1,004 infants; low-certainty evidence) or the incidence of infections per infant (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.42; 3 studies, 500 infants; low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, avoiding the use of bottles for supplementary feeding in preterm infants likely increases the extent of any breastfeeding at discharge and may improve both any and full breastfeeding up to six months post-discharge. Most of the evidence supporting these benefits comes from studies on cup feeding. Only one study evaluated a tube feeding strategy, and the evidence is insufficient to determine whether this approach improves breastfeeding outcomes. Further high-certainty studies are needed to clarify the effects of tube feeding as a supplement to breastfeeding.
